name: Duelist
description:
The blade comes up and the room narrows to a single point of attention—the line between you and the person across from you. Everything else recedes: the crowd, the noise, the stakes. There is only footwork, timing, and the correct next move. You already know what it is. You've done this before.

Duelists are masters of personal combat who have elevated the art of the sword beyond mere survival into a discipline of constant refinement and studied execution. Where soldiers fight with numbers and force, a Duelist invests in precision: careful footwork, crisply timed strikes, and a studied attention to form. To the Duelist, every exchange is more than a physical contest—it is a test of character, technique, and willpower.

Central to every Duelist's practice is the concept of good form: the composure, exactness, and presence of mind that distinguishes a trained master from a desperate fighter. Maintaining form in the heat of battle is its own reward, sharpening focus and building the momentum to press opponents harder with each exchange. When a Duelist is fully in their element, every won engagement feeds that momentum—and momentum itself becomes a weapon. A Duelist who has held their ground patiently can suddenly release that stockpile of poise in a devastating lunge or a perfectly timed coup de grâce.

The Duelist is also a creature of honor, or at least its performance. A favored tactic is the deliberate demand for satisfaction: using force of personality and social confidence to compel one's opponent into undivided attention, making them abandon all others on the field of battle. This isn't manipulation, exactly—it's a kind of contest fought in the space between two gazes before the first blade is drawn.

Duelists favor light weapons, light armor, and swift footwork, trading the protection of heavier gear for freedom of movement. Their engagements are fought with many small dice: reading an opponent through a feint, controlling distance with a compass step, deflecting a blow outright with a parry, or slipping back out of reach with a controlled retreat. Those who value a measure of extra defense without sacrificing agility may add a buckler to their off hand—or a second blade altogether, opening the door to relentless follow-up attacks whenever the first thrust falls short. In any form, dueling is a dialogue at blade's edge, every move an argument that demands a response.

Play a Duelist if you want to:

  • Fight with precision and style, building momentum through disciplined engagement and spending it at the perfect moment.

  • Demand to be met as an equal, using composure and bearing to compel opponents to face you and you alone.

  • Read and outmaneuver your opponents, answering every attack with technique and timing rather than raw strength.

Questions to consider when making a Duelist:

  • Who trained them? Do they follow a particular school of swordsmanship, or have they developed their own style through years of hard experience?

  • What does good form mean to them personally—a source of pride, a survival skill, a kind of aesthetic devotion, or all three?

  • What first drew them to dueling? An affair of honor, the influence of a mentor, a need to prove themselves, or simply a love of the craft?

  • Do they carry that sense of honor into the rest of their life, or is the dueling ground the only place they hold themselves to a higher standard?

  • Have they ever lost a duel that truly mattered? What did it cost them, and what did it teach them?
